title: Public Opinion on Private Funding of Public Elections
citation: Gaines, Brian J., James G. Gimpel, and Andrew Reeves. 2026. "Public Opinion on Private Funding of Public Elections." State and Local Government Review, 1-9. https://doi.org/10.1177/0160323X261469253.
card_summary: Americans are wary of private election-administration funding, while arguments for and against bans produce only modest changes in opinion.
abstract: More than half of American states have sharply limited or banned private donations to public entities for the purpose of supporting election administration. Such legislation is largely consistent with public opinion: Americans are more wary than supportive of such funding, with support for outright bans about as strong as support for regulation, leaving very few who endorse an unregulated, laissez-faire approach. There is, however, a good-sized pool of undecided individuals, who might be nudged into the pro- or anti-ban camps by persuasive arguments. Our evidence, however, is that neither the main pro- nor the main anti- argument vetted in debates to date moves opinion dramatically, though the anti-ban argument might be a little more effective.
plain_english_summary: Most Americans prefer banning or regulating private donations to election administrators rather than leaving them unrestricted, though many remain undecided. Survey experiments conducted before and after the 2024 election show that common arguments on either side generally move opinion only modestly.
research_question: What does the American public think about private funding of election administration, and can prominent pro-ban or anti-ban arguments change those opinions?
research_highlights: Americans are more wary than supportive of private funding for election administration, with substantial support for both bans and regulation.
Very few respondents support allowing private election-administration donations without regulation.
A large share of respondents remain undecided about the issue.
The anti-ban argument has a small persuasive effect, while the tested pro-ban argument has little consistent effect.
methods: Two survey experiments randomly assigned respondents to receive a pro-ban argument, an anti-ban argument, both arguments, or neither argument.
Weighted comparisons of response distributions and regression models estimated treatment effects before and after the 2024 election.
data_sources: The American Social Survey fielded by NORC, August 1-9, 2024 (1,031 American adults)
Post-election Cooperative Election Study survey fielded by YouGov in November 2024 (2,000 American adults)
key_variables: Support for banning private election-administration funding
Support for regulating private election-administration funding
Residence in a state with a ban
identification_strategy: Random assignment to pro-ban, anti-ban, both-argument, or no-argument experimental conditions identifies the persuasive effects of the tested arguments.
policy_relevance: The study informs debates in states considering whether to ban, regulate, or permit private donations to election administrators.
pull_quote: Americans are more wary than supportive of such funding, with support for outright bans about as strong as support for regulation
